claims.text: Structural and chemical stability over 473–1923 K is governed by competition between configurational-entropy stabilization and diffusion-driven phase segregation.
Near-equiatomic incorporation of many elements produces high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically favors a single-phase solid solution.
Temperature-induced atomic diffusion favors phase segregation.
Mixing enthalpies affect whether a high-entropy solid solution decomposes into multiple phases.
Minimal atomic-size mismatch produces lower atomic diffusion rates.
Larger atomic-size mismatch makes diffusion significantly faster.
Nanoparticles with larger atomic-size mismatch cross a critical diffusion threshold and begin to segregate or chemically order.
Changing composition or annealing temperature can cause high-entropy alloys to decompose into multiple phases.
At lower temperatures, configurational entropy stabilizes the single-phase solid solution.
Increasing temperature enhances atomic mobility enough to overcome the entropic mixing benefit.
Nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size mismatch and favorable mixing enthalpies will remain single-phase and chemically homogeneous during heating.
Nanoparticles with higher atomic-size mismatch will develop secondary phases or chemical ordering at temperatures where diffusion accelerates.
Reactive high-temperature atmospheres can cause oxidation, elemental depletion, and phase formation independently of the proposed size-mismatch mechanism.
Microstructural defects and surface effects may influence nanoparticle stability.
In situ high-temperature XRD can identify time- and temperature-dependent phase transformations.

contradictions.description: The comparison is said to vary only atomic-size mismatch and to use particles otherwise identical, but mismatch is changed by varying elemental composition; this will generally also change mixing enthalpy and other chemical properties, so the proposed control does not isolate diffusion kinetics.

The conditions include reactive or oxidizing atmospheres while also asserting that compositional modulation of diffusion is the dominant variable and that severe oxidation should be minimized. Oxidation is itself a composition-dependent mechanism capable of causing elemental depletion and phase changes.
